problem: Prior object-search methods use purely spatial exploration or static semantic maps, and flat LLM/VLM planners cannot chain commonsense relations (room -> furniture -> part) to guide a mobile manipulator in unfamiliar environments. Physical exploration of a carrier (base + end-effector poses) is also inefficient.
motivation: Humans search hierarchically using semantic priors (pillows lie on beds) instead of scanning everything. LLM commonsense combined with segmentation could prune the search space, but LLM outputs are unreliable (hallucination) and the mobile manipulator's pose space is large, so both reasoning and motion need structure.
key_idea: Use an LLM to rank options at a five-level hierarchy (scene, room, carrier, feature, item) under structured prompts, and execute the search with a heuristic pose planner using polar-angle sorting for chassis poses and lexicographic sorting for end-effector poses.
insight: Semantic hierarchical guidance greatly reduces the fraction of the environment searched compared with coverage and random search (OSR 21.03 and 22.61 vs 60.51 and 51.75). The sorting ablation shows that EE sorting and CH sorting each fix their own path ratio, and combining them gives the lowest execution time (0.66 of unoptimized). Both an open 7B LLM and GPT-4o work, so the hierarchy and constraints matter more than the specific model.
method: Five-level hierarchy: scene -> room -> carrier -> feature (top/bottom/sides/inside) -> item; at each level the LLM ranks candidates by P(candidate | set, target) and the agent visits them in order.
Scene exploration and room inference: the robot maps rooms with LiDAR, merges them into a global map, and the LLM infers each room category from semantic-segmentation objects.
Carrier classification and ranking: the LLM filters detected objects to plausible carriers of the target and ranks them; a focused scan captures each carrier point cloud.

Structured LLM reasoning: multi-stage query with input cleaning, core reasoning, and output correction; prompts constrain outputs to a fixed set, include examples, and enforce a machine-readable format to limit hallucination.

Geometric feature extraction and pose generation: top, side, bottom and inside features are derived from the carrier point cloud and occupancy grid; greedy FoV-coverage selects EE poses, greedy geometric selection picks chassis poses, and Levenberg-Marquardt IK validates CH-EE pairs.
Pose sorting: chassis poses are sorted by centroid-aligned polar angle so the base moves around the carrier; EE poses per chassis are sorted lexicographically by (z, y, x, yaw, pitch, roll).

setting.backbone: Qwen2.5-7B and GPT-4o (frozen LLMs, via local Ollama server for Qwen)
setting.observation: LiDAR + RGB camera (RealSense D435) with semantic segmentation; carrier point clouds
setting.action_space: Mobile manipulator base navigation to chassis poses (ROS Navigation Stack) and Franka arm EE poses (MoveIt); high-level LLM-ranked choices
setting.privileged: Semantic segmentation from the simulator; full occupancy map built by exploring all rooms first

numbers.extra: 81 experiments pooled across Qwen2.5-7B and GPT-4o in a simulated flat with seven zones; lower is better; the scene is fully mapped first

numbers_note: Only a single custom simulated scene was evaluated, with no standard benchmark. Table 3 (sorting ablation: EE ratio 1.77, CH ratio 1.59, time ratio 0.66 for both optimized) is not included as a benchmark row.
results: GODHS with GPT-4o reaches an Overall Search Rate of 21.03% and with Qwen2.5-7B 22.61%, versus 60.51% for Coverage and 51.75% for Random search. Combined pose sorting cuts normalized EE path length from 2.81 to 1.77 and CH path length from 2.37 to 1.59, with execution time down to 0.66 of unoptimized.
limitations: Evaluated only in one simulated flat scene, with no real robot and no standard benchmark or learned baselines.
Failures come from hardware reach limits, LLM commonsense errors (e.g. inspecting a non-openable fridge panel) and semantic ambiguity; the scene is fully mapped before searching.
